title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory- Revised-Parent (ChOCI-R-P)
text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) is a 38-item parent-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by a parent or caregiver who is familiar with the child’s experiences. There is also a self-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-S ) that can be completed by children or adolescents aged 7 to 17 years.
6 minutes
Ages 7 to 17 years

title: How should I interpret a profile where Symptoms and Impairment scores diverge?
text: Symptoms and Impairment measure related but distinct dimensions: how often and how strongly symptoms are present, and how much they disrupt daily life. The two can move independently and the gap itself is informative. Where symptoms are elevated but impairment is lower, possible explanations include early presentation, effective coping strategies, or family routines that accommodate symptoms in ways that buffer functional impact. The reverse profile (lower symptoms with elevated impairment) may indicate that the symptoms present are particularly entrenched or distressing, or that the parent is observing functional effects without fully identifying the underlying symptoms. Both divergent profiles warrant looking beyond the totals during formulation.

title: How should I interpret a large gap between the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child-rated ChOCI-R-S?
text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

title: Can the ChOCI-R-P be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
text: The ChOCI-R-P is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. One small treatment study has used it with children as young as 5 (Chessell et al., 2024). Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range. The reference sample included 18-year-olds, so the measure can be used at this age, though a self-report adult measure such as the OCI-R may be more appropriate.

title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-P administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
text: For active CBT-with-Exposure and Response Prevention, parent-rated ChOCI-R-P administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether observable rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence. Trial protocols have used both weekly and pre/post/3-month schedules.

title: Should I use the ChOCI-R-P alongside the child-report version?
text: Yes, where the child is able to complete a self-report. The parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child self-rated ChOCI-R-S are most powerful when used together: administering both at initial assessment gives the clinician a multi-informant baseline that supports more confident formulation and treatment planning. During active treatment, the two measures can be used flexibly. Weekly or fortnightly ChOCI-R-P is the typical pattern for tracking observable change, with periodic ChOCI-R-S to check whether the child’s own experience is shifting alongside the behavioural picture. For younger children who cannot reliably self-report, the ChOCI-R-P alone remains a strong progress-monitoring tool.

title: How are the severity descriptors set, and what do they mean?
text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score.
The lowest impairment band, called “subclinical” on the CY-BOCS, is labelled “Minimal” in NovoPsych because the reference sample is children attending an OCD clinic. The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement.

title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) General Overview
text:
OCD in children and adolescents is characterised by recurrent unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) that the child feels compelled to perform. If untreated, paediatric OCD is associated with substantial functional impairment in academic, social and family domains and tends to persist into adulthood (Heyman et al., 2006). Reliable measurement of severity in young people is challenging because children may under-report or over-report their symptoms during clinical interview, and parents often have observable information about compulsions (washing, checking, ordering) that the child cannot articulate. A parent-report measure offers a useful complement to a child-report, particularly for younger children and for tracking change over time.
The ChOCI-R-P comprises six scored outputs across two construct dimensions:
1. Compulsion Symptoms: frequency and presence of compulsive behaviours (hand-washing, checking, ordering, counting, reassurance-seeking)
2. Obsession Symptoms: frequency and presence of intrusive thoughts (harm, contamination, doubt, blasphemy, aggression)
3. Total Symptoms: overall complexity and pervasiveness of OCD symptomatology
4. Compulsion Impairment: functional disruption from compulsions (time spent, interference, distress, resistance, control, avoidance)
5. Obsession Impairment: equivalent functional disruption from obsessions
6. Total Impairment: overall OCD-related functional disruption
Example ChOCI-R-P Item

title: Clinical Application of the ChOCI-R-P
text: The measure is designed for use with children and adolescents who have an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD. Its primary application is progress monitoring during treatment for paediatric OCD, where pre-treatment, mid-treatment and post-treatment scores can be compared to track symptom reduction and functional improvement. The subscale structure of the ChOCI-R-P can also guide where a clinician focuses exposure hierarchies and cognitive intervention. Additionally, the measure can inform formulation, where the symptom and impairment profile contributes to a broader case conceptualisation alongside diagnostic interview and child-report data.

title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) Scoring
text:
The ChOCI-R-P produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The measure produces two parallel sets of scores: symptoms (how often and how strongly OCD presents) and impairment (how much OCD disrupts daily life).
Total Symptoms : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Symptoms (range 0–40) Compulsion Symptoms : sum of items 1 to 10 (range 0–20) Obsession Symptoms : sum of items 20 to 29 (range 0–20)
Total Impairment : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Impairment (range 0–48) Compulsion Impairment : sum of items 14 to 19 (range 0–24) Obsession Impairment : sum of items 33 to 38 (range 0–24)
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the parent to describe the child’s three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not scored, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

title: ChOCI-R-P Percentiles
text: Each raw score is presented alongside a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample (Uher et al., 2008). A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of OCD-diagnosed children in the reference group. Because the reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a child diagnosed with OCD, not the general paediatric population.

title: ChOCI-R-P Severity Descriptors
text:
Each of the six scores is reported with a severity descriptor alongside its percentile. The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement.
Symptoms (three bands): A Low label (green) indicates a symptom level lower than typical for children with OCD (atypically light for this reference group); Moderate (yellow) indicates a symptom level within the typical range for children with OCD; High (red) indicates a symptom level above the typical OCD-clinical range. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Symptoms cut-offs. Raw-score boundaries:
Total Symptoms : Low ≤10, Moderate 11–26, High ≥27
Compulsion Symptoms : Low ≤5, Moderate 6–14, High ≥15
Obsession Symptoms : Low ≤3, Moderate 4–13, High ≥14
Impairment (five bands): A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for children with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs. Raw-score boundaries:
Total Impairment : Minimal ≤13, Mild 14–23, Moderate 24–33, Severe 34–42, Extreme ≥43
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal ≤7, Mild 8–12, Moderate 13–17, Severe 18–21, Extreme ≥22
Obsession Impairment : Minimal ≤4, Mild 5–10, Moderate 11–16, Severe 17–21, Extreme ≥22

title: ChOCI-R-P Subscale Interpretation
text: Each subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the parent has observed more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, including washing, checking, ordering, counting, repeating, and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, contamination, doubt, mortality, blasphemy, or aggressive content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

title: ChOCI-R-P Change Score Interpretation
text: When the ChOCI-R-P is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 8.4 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

title: ChOCI-R-P Graphs
text:
On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score against a 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average from the OCD-clinical reference sample. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession) with their own reference rectangles and clinical-average lines.


On repeat administration, the report presents the same results table followed by a 2×3 grid of multi-administration raw-score line plots organised by construct: top row Symptoms (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions); bottom row Impairment (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions). Each plot shows one score over time on its own descriptor bands, so the shading behind each point matches that score’s descriptor in the results table. Unlike the first-administration charts, these graphs emphasise longitudinal change rather than position within the clinical reference distribution.

title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) Development
text:
The ChOCI-R has self-report and parent-report forms, developed and validated together (Uher et al., 2008); NovoPsych refers to them as the ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P, and ‘ChOCI-R’ below refers to the instrument as a whole or to findings covering both forms.
The ChOCI-R is a revision of the original CHOCI (Shafran et al., 2003), refined to improve item-level psychometrics and broaden severity coverage. The original CHOCI used 19 symptom items rated on a three-point scale (1 to 3) and a 10-item impairment scale derived from the CY-BOCS interview (Goodman et al., 1989; Scahill et al., 1997), scored 0 to 4. The ChOCI-R retains the 10 best-performing symptom items per section (compulsions and obsessions), changes the symptom response format to a three-option scale scored 0 to 2, and adds an avoidance item to each impairment section to align with the adult Y-BOCS. The remaining five impairment items (time, interference, distress, resistance, control) are unchanged between the original CHOCI and the ChOCI-R (Uher et al., 2008).
Published reports describe the ChOCI-R-P as a 32-item measure (the scored items only). NovoPsych’s version also administers six unscored open-text items describing the child’s worst habits and thoughts, which, like the Y-BOCS symptom checklist, capture specific symptom content to aid formulation, giving 38 items in total.
Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

title: ChOCI-R-P Factor Structure
text: Factor-analytic work supports the use of separate Compulsion and Obsession subscales for clinical interpretation. Exploratory analysis of the ChOCI-R-P recovered three factors broadly corresponding to Compulsions, Obsessions and Resistance, with the parent version showing less clean obsession/compulsion separation than the self-report version (Uher et al., 2008). This pattern is consistent with parents inferring obsessions from observed behaviours rather than directly accessing the child’s internal experience. The NovoPsych scoring approach prioritises the clinically meaningful distinction between compulsive and obsessive content, producing separate Compulsion and Obsession scores at both the Symptoms and Impairment levels.

title: ChOCI-R-P Reliability
text: Internal consistency of the ChOCI-R-P is strong across the four subscales and two totals (Uher et al., 2008). For the impairment scales, Cronbach’s α was .84 (Obsessions Impairment, N = 240), .78 (Compulsions Impairment, N = 269) and .87 (Total Impairment, N = 240). For the symptom scales, α was .86 (Obsession Symptoms, N = 240), .75 (Compulsion Symptoms, N = 269) and .85 (Total Symptoms, N = 240). The lower α for the Compulsion Symptoms scale reflects the heterogeneity of compulsive behaviours, with the hand-washing item showing a low item-total correlation; the authors retained the item to preserve coverage of a clinically common compulsion.

title: ChOCI-R-P Validity
text:
Convergent validity was demonstrated through a moderate correlation between the ChOCI-R-P Total Impairment and the CY-BOCS Total score ( r = 0.45, N = 199, p < .001; Uher et al., 2008). The moderate (rather than strong) correlation, compared with r = 0.55 for the ChOCI-R-S against the CY-BOCS, reflects the partial independence of parent observation and clinician-rated severity in young people.
Inter-rater agreement between ChOCI-R-P and ChOCI-R-S was strong, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69–0.83) for Total Impairment, 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.77) for Obsessions Impairment, and 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.85) for Compulsions Impairment (Uher et al., 2008).
Item-response theory (IRT) analysis demonstrated that the parent-report ChOCI-R-P provides better discrimination across the mild-to-moderate severity range than the CY-BOCS interview, which discriminates best at the most severe end of the spectrum (Uher et al., 2008). This complementary discriminatory profile supports the use of the ChOCI-R-P as a routine outcome measure in clinical practice, where many children present in the mild-to-moderate severity range and finer-grained discrimination is clinically useful.

title: ChOCI-R-P Sensitivity to Change
text: The ChOCI-R-P has demonstrated sensitivity to change in three independent treatment studies spanning the paediatric age range (7 to 17). Lenhard and colleagues (2017) reported a within-group pre-post effect of d = 0.68 (95% CI 0.18–1.18) and a between-group effect of d = 0.59 (95% CI 0.09–1.10) favouring internet-delivered CBT over waitlist in adolescents aged 12 to 17 ( N = 67; p = .012), with continued improvement to a 3-month follow-up. Aspvall and colleagues (2018) reported very large pre-post effects ( d = 2.15, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.20) in a 12-week internet-delivered CBT open trial with young children aged 7 to 11 ( N = 11), with α = .87 in that sample (replicating Uher et al., 2008). Chessell and colleagues (2024) reported large pre-post effects in a parent-led brief CBT case series of pre-adolescents aged 5 to 12 ( N = 10): d ≈ −1.0 for symptoms and d ≈ −1.1 for impairment, with 50% reliable improvement on symptoms and 60% on impairment at post-treatment.

title: ChOCI-R-P Descriptors
text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study. The lowest impairment band, called “subclinical” on the CY-BOCS, is labelled “Minimal” in NovoPsych because the reference sample is children attending an OCD clinic.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 17th percentile and High at about the 85th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 58th and Extreme about the 89th.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997). NovoPsych could not find them in either paper, in the scale authors’ later work, or anywhere else. We therefore treat them as an established clinical convention, and keep them for consistency with common practice and with earlier NovoPsych reports.

title: ChOCI-R-P Sample Data
text:
Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (240 to 269 with complete parent-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ average age = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ average age = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the parent-report subscales are Compulsion Symptoms average = 9.8, SD = 4.5; Obsession Symptoms average = 8.4, SD = 5.2; Total Symptoms average = 18.3, SD = 8.0; Compulsion Impairment average = 16.5, SD = 4.2; Obsession Impairment average = 15.5, SD = 5.0; Total Impairment average = 32.1, SD = 8.4. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a child diagnosed with OCD, not the general paediatric population. No community-sample reference data exists for the parent-report ChOCI-R-P, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).
